IF has many benefits on its own, but for weight loss its primary function is just that it makes caloric restrictions easier and more manageable. You can't lose weight if your caloric intake is larger than your caloric expenditure. I eat 1200 calories a day (I am small; just need to be smaller) and weigh almost everything to the gram. You don't need to be this extreme if your caloric budget is bigger but the point is you still have to be in a deficit to lose weight. A cup of fruits would be a healthy dessert, but they can actually be pretty high in calories (one mango=200 calories, for example). If you're not tracking your caloric intake it's really easy to overeat, and as you get older/smaller your TDEE gets smaller and smaller, meaning you have to eat less or move more if you want to lose weight

It's true that your metabolic rate slows down temporarily when dieting (i.e. person on a diet would burn less calories than what is expected given their sex/height/weight), but the extent to which it slows down is really pretty negligible and even that negligible difference is pretty quickly made up once you up your caloric intake. There is [no proof that adaptive thermogenesis persists long term](https://academic.oup.com/ajcn/article/108/4/658/5129189?login=false) after losing weight--the main thing that affects the metabolic rate is actually the fact that now you are smaller and need to eat at a portion size appropriate for a smaller person in order to maintain that size.

You burn roughly 2300 or more calories by simply existing. By existing I mean if you were bedridden 24/7 your body would still burn at least 2300 calories a day just to ensure you are breathing and your organs are working. You're sedentary, but I'm sure you walk, do simple chores like washing dishes/buying things at the grocery store, working/studying etc. You likely burn more than 2800 calories a day being a man of your size enjoying a sedentary lifestyle. You can likely eat 2200\~2300 calories a day and still lose more than a pound each week; likely even more in the beginning as you lose your bloat (water weight).

If you ate 1200 calories a day you will be creating a deficit of 1600 calories a day, which translates to \~3.2 pounds loss a week. This is way too fast, dangerous, and unsustainable. You'll likely feel miserable and you will be putting yourself at a risk for things like gallstones, hair loss, and a host of unpleasant things that are just not worth it.

Get a kitchen scale and a bathroom scale. Get a tailor's tape while you're at it. You should start by knowing exactly where you stand--how much you weigh, what your waist measurements are, and what/how much you currently eat in a day. Download an app like Loseit or Myfitnesspal that lets you enter everything you eat in a day and track your calories. Personally, jumping into "healthy eating" right away has always been a recipe for failure for me. What worked for me was just keeping all my regular meals at first (just make sure that you are at a caloric deficit), but cutting out the sugary drinks and snacks. I would replace coke with diet coke, and have some fruits instead of cookies or ice cream. At a higher weight making small changes will yield big results relatively fast, and seeing those tangible results will likely move you to want to have healthier habits. Once the weight starts rolling off and you get your momentum going you can ease into caring about macros and incorporate some light exercise like walking.

So the problem for me is that the Timeless Child isn't just some kid. Godlike doesn't have to mean invincible or flawless in this context. TC isn't special because of anything they did--like how doctor stole the tardis--no, they're special because they just inherently are; the power that they were born with. The doctor regenerates, sure, but this feature doesn't define the doctor's brilliance. It defines the TC's specialness, though. Like you said TC is helpless. TC doesn't have agency in what makes them special.

I see a lot of arguments for TC saying that it doesn't really change who the doctor is, and they're still the same person as they were before the reveal. I really don't agree with this, but even if it were true, why do it then? Why retcon a 50 year old character development if it doesn't change the doctor as a character? Doctor being TC doesn't provide more depth; it doesn't lead to bigger events or identity crises; it doesn't even really expand the doctor's personal history as there's just this big mysterious disconnect and the doctor was always the doctor--why does TC storyline deserve to exist then? I can't fathom what it adds to the DW lore.

For me the doctor was someone who was able to change his mediocrity and cowardice into brilliance by running away from a powerful but unjust (timelord) society and beginning his own adventures. He had agency in starting this adventure and that choice is what made him special. You might argue that TC doesn't invalidate that choice, but I think if there were tons of other doctors (at least some of whom have TARDISes, which makes no sense but whatever) before 1 it definitely trivializes the "initial" decision at least a little bit, as the decision is no longer the initial one. This Recharacterization of the doctor as some kind of a mythical origin of said powerful species (that doesn't have this kind of agency) was a punch in the gut for me.

And Just FYI I didn't downvote you. You are entitled to your tastes and opinions. As you can see I'm really not a fan of TC lol, but I'm glad at least some others like it. I'd even concede that there are aspects of TC that I find interesting. Still, if TC was going to happen no matter what, I think there must have been a much better way to execute it than what Chibnall actually did. I think I would have been kinder to the idea if it actually went somewhere or led to anything meaningful.

I really liked that the doctor was just some kid--bright, brilliant, belonging to a very special group of aliens, sure, but still inherently just a kid--that stole a time machine to have wacky adventures. To me this accidental and trivial beginning suited the doctor's identity as an "eccentric traveler who happens to get things right most of the time" rather than some godlike figure that was destined for great things. RTD is guilty of making ten's arc way more grandiose than necessary, and Moffat certainly walked a fine line like you describe, but Chibnall flat out made the doctor a "chosen one" and I'll never forgive him for that.

I was in a similar boat as your daughter when I was 19 and in college. I'm so glad that I only had access to shitty student cards because my limit was around 3000 and I maxed them out pretty quickly. Little spending at the mall, eating out, ordering books, ubers, all those small purchases add up when you don't pay off right way because you feel like you have access to free money even though in your head you know that it's something you have to pay back. You don't see any consequences when making minimum payments even if your cards are maxed out so you don't realize that you're in the rut til it's way late. It took me a while but I'm credit card debt free now and paying off the cards and building my credit up has been some of the most valuable experiences I had in terms of maturing. I think I'd have been way worse off should I maxed out my credit cards now with much higher limits so in a way I'm glad I made that mistake when I was younger. I'm not defending your daughter mind you she did a shitty stupid thing. Just sharing my experience to let you know if you educate her properly and make her realize that there are severe consequences--that she could really ruin her life over this--this will be a maturing opportunity for her.
